chapter_theme: Nineteen of the twenty verses name about six marks of a giver (refusals of killing, flesh, toddy, lies and theft, and gifts of food, goods, water works and cures to the ruined, the sick, mothers and ascetics) and pay each with a reward, mostly kingship in a later life; the run closes with a learner's six habits and the six evils of bad company.

41.reading: The verse names six marks of a man (he does not draw near the mean, does not take flesh, does not stray into falsehood, does not seize others' goods, is not close-fisted, and gives to those who have no means) and says that, if he is such, the books of the path will recite his worth beyond measure.
41.nuance: The reward is not a rebirth but praise in the texts themselves (நெறிநூல்கள் ... பன்னும்): the giver becomes a subject the books recite. The last two items turn from refusals to giving: not being tight (இறுகான்) and giving to the resourceless.

items.claim: he does not draw near the mean
he does not take flesh
he does not wander in falsehood
he does not seize what belongs to others
he is not close-fisted
he gives to those who have nothing to fall back on

norm.note: the Jain abstention from flesh of the period, counted among a giver's marks

42.reading: The verse says that one who does not kill, does not consent to killing, does not join the company of killers, does not cling to what is others', does not stray into the delusion of flesh, and has fed people, settling them in households, will rule the earth as a king, mounted on a killing elephant, bringing foes under his feet.
42.nuance: The non-killer's reward is a killing elephant (கொல்யானை) and enemies trodden under: the verse sees no strain in paying non-violence with conquest. புல்லான் பிறர்பால் may mean not embracing another's wife or not attaching himself to others; குடிப்படுத்து may be 'settling families' or 'establishing his own house'.

items.claim: he does not kill
he does not consent to killing
he does not join the company of killers
he does not cling to what belongs to others
he does not go into the delusion of flesh
he gave food, settling people in households

norm.note: the Jain rule against killing and flesh of the period, extended to consenting and to company

43.reading: Addressing a woman with long makara earrings, the verse says that one who does not delight in gambling, does not swerve, does not speak deceit, does not relish disputes with anyone, does not trust women's words, and has given food to great ascetics will dwell in a mansion with makara-mouthed ornament.
43.nuance: The makara of the woman's earring returns as the makara mouths of the reward mansion, a verbal rhyme of the frame. பேரான் (does not move away) and கலா(வு) (theft, or a form of கலாம், strife) are unsure. The distrust of women's words recurs in verses 5 and 20.

items.claim: he does not delight in gambling
he does not swerve from his place
he does not speak deceit or strife
he does not relish disputing with anyone
he does not trust the words of women
he has given food to great ascetics

norm.note: a rule of the period that a man of virtue does not trust women's words

44.reading: The verse says that one who does not lie, does not take to falsehood, does not eat flesh, does not revile anyone, clears the road, and gives fine white rice without grudging before he eats will become a king of the sea-girt earth whose lot is to share his food and be praised.
44.nuance: The reward repeats the act: one who gave before eating (ஈத்துண்பான்) becomes a king who shares before eating (பாத்துண்பான்), so kingship is the same virtue on a larger table. Clearing the road (வழிசீத்து) is a public work set among private restraints.

items.claim: he does not lie
he does not take to falsehood
he does not eat flesh
he reviles no one
he clears the road
he gives white rice without grudging before he eats

norm.note: the Jain abstention from flesh of the period, set among a giver's marks

45.reading: The verse says that one who does not slip from the proper way, does not covet harmful things, does not err, does not seize the house and goods of others, walks by right conduct and gives faultless food will rule, conquer, and quickly let go.
45.nuance: விடுப்பான் விரைந்து closes the reward: on one reading the king soon lets the kingdom go, a Jain turn in which rule is a stage before renunciation; on another he quickly releases those he has conquered. மனைபொருள் may be another's house and goods or another's wife and goods.

items.claim: he does not slip from the proper way
he does not covet harmful things
he does not err
he does not seize another's house and goods
he goes by right conduct
he gives faultless food

46.reading: The verse says that if one does not revel, does not drink toddy, does not look upon drinkers, neither hides from nor flinches at guests, does not scorn the poor, and eats only after giving, he will rule a land without harm and his family will thrive abundantly.
46.nuance: Three items circle toddy (revelry, drinking, the sight of drinkers) and three circle the table (guests, the poor, eating after giving), so abstention and hospitality are one portrait. ஒளியான் விருந்துக்(கு) உலையான் is taken as one item; split, it gives seven.

items.claim: he does not revel
he does not drink toddy
he does not look upon those who revel in drink
he neither hides from guests nor wearies of them
he does not scorn the poor
he eats only after giving

norm.note: the period's rule against toddy, extended to the sight of drinkers

47.reading: The verse says that one who keeps the words of the great and stands without swerving, does not despoil servants who do not desert him, does not trust the words of the black-hearted, does not join them, gives food with a clear mind before he eats, and does not change, will rule the earth.
47.nuance: பரியா அடியார் is unsure: servants who do not run off, or the unpitied poor at one's feet. கரியார் may be the black-hearted or, since கரி is a witness, false witnesses.

items.claim: he keeps the words of the great and stands without swerving
he does not despoil the servants who stay by him
he does not trust the words of the black-hearted
he does not join with them
he gives food with a clear mind before he eats
he does not change

48.reading: The verse says that if a man does not join in strangers' clamour, does not turn away guests, calls out the sound of the meal in his house before he eats, does not listen to hostile talk, and cherishes his kin, he will come as an unfailing king ruling the earth by the sword.
48.nuance: Three அரவம் words (sound) carry the verse: strangers' noise he avoids, the rice-call he makes, hostile noise he will not hear. Calling out before eating makes the meal public. Five things, not six; கிளைஓம்பின் is counted as the fifth.

items.claim: he does not join in strangers' clamour
he does not turn away guests
he announces the meal in his house before he eats
he does not listen to hostile talk
he cherishes his kin

49.reading: The verse names elephants, horses, gold, a maiden, herds of cattle and all other gifts besides, and says that one who, with these in mind, gave food with cow's ghee to great ascetics will live as Vaisravana, the lord of wealth.
49.nuance: The relation of the list to the food gift turns on எண்ணனாய்: either the food with ghee is reckoned as worth all these great gifts, or the giver gave all these and food as well. On the first reading the verse ranks a meal for ascetics above the royal gift catalogue. The maiden (கன்னி) stands in a list of goods given.

items.claim: an elephant is one of the great gifts weighed against the food
a horse is one of the great gifts
gold is one of the great gifts
a maiden given in marriage is one of the great gifts
herds of cattle are one of the great gifts
all the remaining gifts are counted with them

norm.note: a period gift-list that counts a maiden given in marriage among goods given away

50.reading: The verse says that one who gave sesame, cotton, oil, cloth to wear, a vessel and cloth, and with them food given with love, saying 'take it', will live happily joined with his companion.
50.nuance: The goods are household stuffs, and the reward is household joy: a life with one's partner. வள் is unsure (a vessel or a measure), and உடுத்தாடை and துணி may both be cloth, one worn and one uncut.

items.claim: sesame is given with the food
cotton is given
oil is given
cloth to wear is given
a vessel is given
cloth is given

51.reading: The verse says that one who made over to common use a tank rich in drinking water, a well, a wayside shelter, a water-booth and a public hall will live abundantly amid tuneful song and dance, in love's union and its quarrels.
51.nuance: The reward is pleasure, not heaven or kingship: music, dance, and the akam pair of union and sulking (கூடல், ஊடல்). Five works are counted; உண்ணீர் வளம் could be read as a sixth (a source of drinking water) rather than as the tank's quality.

items.claim: a tank rich in drinking water, made over to common use
a well made over to common use
a wayside shelter made over to common use
a water-booth made over to common use
a public hall made over to common use

52.reading: The verse says that those who toil by day to cook and feed people who have lost their house, their eyes, their gathered wealth, their paddy or their herds will become kings with many elephants and eat with considered plenty.
52.nuance: Every recipient is defined by a loss (இழந்தார் five times), so the list is a census of ruin: blindness sits among the losses of house, grain and cattle. Five things.

items.claim: those who have lost their house are fed
those who have lost their eyes are fed
those who have lost their gathered wealth are fed
those who have lost their paddy are fed
those who have lost their herds are fed

53.reading: The verse says that those who, consenting and having the means, feed in their own houses the indebted, the unprotected, those with nothing in hand, the lame, the old and the young will live on earth as masters of armies.
53.nuance: The feeding is in the house (இல்லுள்), not at a public charity. தங்கான் is read as தம் கால் (their own legs) before முடம்பட்டார்; மூப்பில்லார் may be the young or those with no elders to keep them.

items.claim: the indebted are fed in the house
those without protection are fed
those with nothing in hand are fed
those lamed in their legs are fed
the old are fed
the young, or those without elders, are fed

54.reading: The verse says that those who, without calculating, gave food to brahmins, the hungry, ascetics, children and those who have no one at all to protect them will rule the earth with a full treasury.
54.nuance: பார்ப்பார் is a caste term, here naming brahmins by birth as a class of fit recipients, set first beside the hungry and the unprotected. The end of line 2 and start of line 3 (தூப்பால நிண்டாரால்) are corrupt; a sixth recipient may be hidden there.

items.claim: brahmins are among those fed
the hungry are fed
ascetics are fed
children are fed
those who have no one at all to protect them are fed

norm.note: a period list of fit recipients that names brahmins by birth (பார்ப்பார்) first

55.reading: The verse says that those who, treating them as their own, fed and relieved the grave ills of women who have given birth, those weakened at delivery, the pregnant, infants, the distraught and those stricken by wind-disease will live joined with great wealth.
55.nuance: Four of the six recipients belong to the birth-room (mothers, those weak in labour, the pregnant, infants), so the verse makes childbirth a field of charity. The giver both feeds and cures (ஊண்ஈய்த்து உறுநோய் களைந்தார்).

items.claim: women who have given birth are fed and tended
those weakened at delivery are fed and tended
pregnant women are fed and tended
infants are fed and tended
the distraught are fed and tended
those stricken by wind-disease are fed and tended

56.reading: Addressing a woman with a deer's glance, the verse says that those who, as kin, gave food to those who were heads of houses, the distressed, the fallen, women, the toiling poor and those with no food at all will rule the island of Jambu girt by the great sea.
56.nuance: Line 2's உயை஡ளர் is corrupt (an unassigned code point) and several words (தாப்பாளர், ஊண்ஈய்ந்தபர், மாக்கடால்) look miscopied, so the recipients after the first are guesses. The reward, rule of நாவலம்தீவு, is the widest in the chapter.

items.claim: those who were heads of houses are fed
the distressed are fed
the fallen are fed
women are fed
the toiling poor (a corrupt word) are fed
those with no food at all are fed

57.reading: The verse says that those who took hard pains to feed and cure sufferers of black scab, white leprosy, stone, wind-disease, burning great sores and the fire of a swollen belly will become kings who protect and eat in honour.
57.nuance: Divided into six by reading கல்வளி as stone and wind-disease and காயும் as qualifying the great sores; read கல்வளி as one ailment and the count is five. The giver here is a healer as well as a feeder (அவை தீர்த்தார்).

items.claim: those with black scab are fed and cured
those with white leprosy are fed and cured
those with stone are fed and cured
those with wind-disease are fed and cured
those with burning great sores are fed and cured
those with the fire of a swollen belly are fed and cured

58.reading: The verse says that those who do not sport in lust, do not desire, do not join the unlearned, do not say yes lightly, stand in the way of those who have inquired, and, without boasting, gave to those who asked so that they rejoiced, will in this very life overcome their enemies.
58.nuance: The reward is in this life (இம்மையான்), where most verses of the run look to a later birth. காமாடார் and ஆமாடார் are obscure; the second may be 'do not dance to every yes'. ஆயந்தார் is read as ஆய்ந்தார்.

items.claim: they do not sport in lust
they do not desire
they do not join the company of the unlearned
they do not assent lightly
they stand in the way of those who have inquired
they gave to those who asked so that they rejoiced

59.reading: The verse says that one who bows, follows the right way, takes the words of the excellent, studies the subtle books and penetrates them, and lives attending to what is fitting will live as a blameless king, examining the books closely.
59.nuance: The only verse of the run without a gift of food: the six things are a learner's acts, and the reward, a blameless king who still reads (நூல்நோக்கி), returns to the study of line 2. நுழையா is read as the old participle 'having entered'.

items.claim: he bows to the worthy
he follows the right way
he takes the words of the excellent
he studies the subtle books
he penetrates them
he attends to what is fitting

60.reading: The verse says that if one draws near those without worth, who neglect greatness, fame and virtue, are given to anger and lack the rare books, then sin, blame, enmity, death, ruin and fear will cling to him in both worlds like a curse.
60.nuance: Line 1 may describe the unworthy (neglecting greatness, fame and virtue) or list what is lost by the company. கேடச்சம் joins ruin and fear in one word, so the five items counted here are six evils; 'both worlds' (இருமைக்கும்) makes the cost run past this life.

items.claim: sin clings to one who keeps bad company
blame clings to him
enmity clings to him
death clings to him
ruin and fear cling to him

links.note: Kural 232 says all that speakers say amounts to praise resting on those who give to askers; verse 41 says the books of the path will recite the worth of one who gives to the resourceless.
links.teaches: The couplet locates fame in what people say; the verse places it in the scriptures themselves, so giving earns a place in the texts that teach giving.
links.list_adds: It makes giving the last of six marks after five refusals (the mean, flesh, falsehood, theft, tight-fistedness), so the praise in the books is earned by a whole discipline and not by the gift alone.

links.note: Kural 260 says all beings worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; verse 42 widens the refusal to consenting to killing and to the company of killers, and rewards it with kingship on a killing elephant.
links.teaches: The couplet's reward is the reverence of the spared creatures; the verse pays the same abstention with conquest, showing a Jain work content to reward non-killing with a war elephant.
links.list_adds: It splits the couplet's one refusal into three degrees of complicity (killing, consenting, keeping killers' company) and then joins them to feeding, so non-killing is graded by distance from the act.

links.note: Kural 908 says those who act as a woman wishes fail their friends and do no good; verse 43 sets not trusting women's words beside feeding great ascetics, both as a giver's marks.
links.teaches: Read together, the period rule against heeding women is tied in both works to giving: the Kural says it stops good deeds, and Elathi sets it beside the meal for ascetics it protects.
links.list_adds: It puts distrust of women's words among gambling, deceit and disputes, as one more distraction a giver must refuse, where the Kural's chapter treats it alone as a fault of the husband.

links.note: Kural 322 calls sharing one's food and sustaining many lives the chief of all virtues; verse 44's giver, who gives white rice before eating, is reborn a king whose lot is to share and eat.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks sharing first among virtues; the verse makes it also the shape of the reward, so the king of the next birth is the sharer of this one on a larger scale.
links.list_adds: It sets sharing after truthfulness, refusing flesh, not reviling and clearing the road, so the couplet's chief virtue closes a list that joins speech, diet and public work.

links.note: Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time; verse 45, on the reading that விடுப்பான் is letting the kingdom go, says the giver will rule, conquer and quickly give it up.
links.teaches: On that reading the verse makes kingship a stage on the way to renunciation, a reward meant to be left, where the couplet speaks of renouncing what one already has.
links.list_adds: It sets renunciation at the end of a reward sequence (rule, conquest, release) earned by six marks of conduct, so the couplet's counsel becomes the last step of a karmic career.

links.note: Kural 922 says not to drink and, if one does, to be one who does not care for the esteem of the worthy; verse 46 bars not only drinking but looking upon drinkers.
links.teaches: The couplet treats drink as the drinker's own loss of standing; the verse extends the bar to the sight of drinkers, so the rule reaches the company one keeps.
links.list_adds: It sets three degrees of avoiding toddy (revelry, drinking, seeing drinkers) beside three duties of the table, so abstention is joined to hospitality as one portrait of the householder.

links.note: Kural 527 says crows do not hide but call out and eat, and gain belongs to those of that nature; verse 48 counts announcing the meal in one's house before eating as a mark of the future king.
links.teaches: The verse gives the crow's call a human form, a spoken rice-call (சோற்றரவம்) in the house, and shows the couplet's image was a practice before it was a figure.
links.list_adds: It plays the rice-call against two other noises the householder avoids (strangers' clamour, hostile talk), so the sound he makes is defined by the sounds he refuses.

links.note: Naladiyar 271 says sharing what is cooked before eating is true cooking, and the door of the next world shuts on those who shut the door and eat; verse 48 has the householder call out the meal and rewards him with kingship.
links.teaches: The two give the same act opposite outcomes: the closed door and closed heaven in the Naladiyar, the public rice-call and a sword-held kingdom in Elathi, so the meal's openness decides the next life in both.
links.list_adds: It makes the open meal one of five household marks, with keeping guests and cherishing kin, where the quatrain argues the single act with a punishment.

links.note: Iniyavai Narpathu 23 calls giving gold with cows to brahmins foremost sweet; verse 49 names gold and herds among great gifts and sets with them food with ghee for great ascetics.
links.teaches: The same gifts of gold and cattle are aimed at brahmins in Iniyavai and joined to a meal for ascetics in Elathi, showing the two codes differ on who is the worthy recipient.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 65 says one who digs a tank, sets its bank, clears a road, breaks a field and digs a shared well goes sweetly to heaven; verse 51 rewards tanks, wells, shelters, water-booths and halls with a life of music, dance and love.
links.teaches: Two Jain works price the same public water works differently: heaven in one, sensual pleasure and the akam play of union and sulking in the other.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 72 says a mouthful given unasked to the weak, the old, those fasting to death, the sick and those who lost their land makes the giver a king; verse 52 makes kings of those who feed people who lost house, eyes, wealth, paddy or herds.
links.teaches: The two works state one rule, food to the ruined earns kingship, but Elathi defines need wholly by loss while Sirupanchamoolam includes the dying ascetic, so they draw the circle of the needy differently.

links.note: Kural 226 says removing the hunger of the destitute is where a man with wealth should store it; verse 53 names six kinds of destitute to be fed in the house and pays the store back as command of armies.
links.teaches: The couplet's metaphor of storage is made literal: the verse says what the stored wealth returns as, an army in a later life.
links.list_adds: It breaks the couplet's one class of the destitute into six (the indebted, unprotected, empty-handed, lame, old and young), so need is named by its causes.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 7 says the பார்ப்பான் is one who shares his food; verse 54 lists பார்ப்பார் first among those to be fed, beside the hungry and ascetics.
links.teaches: One Jain work defines the brahmin by giving food, the other names brahmins by birth as receivers of it, so the same word marks a giver's virtue in one and a recipient's rank in the other.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 71 calls delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant great virtue; verse 55 counts feeding and curing new mothers, the pregnant and infants as acts that earn great wealth.
links.teaches: Both Jain works make the birth-room a field of merit; Elathi adds food and cure to the care and names a reward where Sirupanchamoolam cites the old books.

links.note: Sirupanchamoolam 75 says those who cured the diseases of five kinds of sufferer live now without disease; verse 57 says those who fed and cured six diseases become kings.
links.teaches: The two works pay the same act of healing differently: Sirupanchamoolam returns it in kind as health, Elathi converts it, like its other gifts, into rule.

links.note: Kural 441 counsels choosing the friendship of those mature in virtue and knowledge; verse 59 sets taking the words of the excellent among a learner's acts and makes them the making of a blameless king.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks to a king choosing counsellors; the verse shows the same habit begun as a learner's discipline of bowing and study, which yields the king.
links.list_adds: It sets taking counsel between bowing and close study, so heeding the great is one of six habits of learning rather than a separate policy of state.

links.note: Kural 460 says nothing brings more affliction than bad company; verse 60 names the afflictions, sin, blame, enmity, death, ruin and fear, and says they cling in both worlds like a curse.
links.teaches: The couplet's 'affliction' is left general; the verse itemises it and extends it beyond this life, so bad company is a karmic cost and not only a social one.
links.list_adds: It counts the evils that follow from bad company and joins worldly ones (blame, enmity) to otherworldly ones (sin), which the couplet's single word does not separate.

56: line 2 has an unassigned Tamil code point (உயை஡ளர், U+0BA1); ஊண்ஈய்ந்தபர் and மாக்கடால் on line 3 look miscopied.
